problems.stem: A team reports 90% satisfaction and concludes "learners are learning." Which classification error did they make?
options: Satisfaction is too small a percentage to report.
They used a usability or attitude metric (satisfaction) to support a learning-outcome claim it cannot measure.
Satisfaction should be reported as a mean, not a percentage.
They needed more than 10 participants for satisfaction.
problems.explanation: Satisfaction measures how the experience felt, not whether knowledge or skill changed; a learning claim needs a learning metric.

problems.stem: Which pairing correctly matches a claim to a metric that can measure it?
options: Claim: the menu is findable. Metric: pre/post quiz gain.
Claim: learners mastered the concept. Metric: average time on task.
Claim: learners can apply the concept to new items. Metric: accuracy on transfer items not seen in the lesson.
Claim: the interface is efficient. Metric: self-reported confidence.
problems.explanation: A transfer claim is supported by performance on novel items; the other pairings attach a metric that measures a different construct.

problems.stem: An AI dashboard auto-summarizes your session data into a single "effectiveness score" blending satisfaction, time, and quiz gain. What is the defensible boundary?
options: Report the blended score because it is convenient and looks rigorous.
Keep the metrics disaggregated; a single blended score hides whether a usability or a learning claim is actually supported.
Trust the AI score over your own metrics.
Delete the quiz data so the score is purely usability.
problems.explanation: Blending distinct constructs into one number obscures which claim the evidence supports; keep usability and learning metrics separate.

problems.stem: Post-test scores rose, but participants also took the test immediately after viewing the answers in the lesson. Why is the learning gain claim still shaky?
options: The sample size was too small.
Without a delay or transfer measure, the gain may reflect short-term recall of just-seen answers rather than durable learning.
Post-tests are never valid learning metrics.
Satisfaction should have been measured instead.
problems.explanation: An immediate post-test can capture recall of fresh content; durable or transferable learning needs a delayed or novel-item measure.
